params.text:
Welcome to This Module

Welcome to The Use of Animals in Research, a learning module developed as part of the BriGRETE project (Bridging the Gap in Research Ethics Training and Education), co-funded by the European Union.

This module provides an overview of the basic principles of ethical animal research and good research practices that produce reliable research. The module provides researchers and IACUC members with a deeper understanding of responsible research practices and the concept of the 3Rs so that research conducted is of high quality, relevant and reliable to the research community and the public, while minimizing harm to the animals used and taking into account their physiological and psychological characteristics.

Learning Objectives

Participants will develop knowledge about usage of animals in research. Specifically, they will gain the following:

  • A knowledge about different views about animal usage in research and their moral basis;
  • An understanding about arguments in dispute of using animals in research;
  • 3R principle;
  • Knowledge about the way in which animals can be ethically used and the regulation of such researches;
  • EU legislation regarding the use of animals for research purposes;
  • Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC).

Target Audience

These groups will benefit from tailored, accessible content that enhances their knowledge, compliance practices, and decision-making abilities in research ethics, contributing to a more inclusive and responsible research community.

  • IACUC Members: Members who review and oversee research projects to ensure ethical and integrity standards are met, including new IACUC members who may benefit from structured, foundational training, as well as experienced IACUC members looking to update their knowledge of current developments in ethics of research with animals.
  • Researchers: Early-career researchers (postgraduate students, PhD candidates, and postdoctoral researchers) who need foundational knowledge in ethics of research with animals. Mid-career and senior researchers who would like to keep updated about responsible animal research, especially those engaging with advanced ethical issues in areas like AI, data management, and interdisciplinary research.

Estimated Duration

Approximately 60–90 minutes, depending on your pace and engagement with the interactive activities.

params.text:
Introduction

Animal experimentation is one of the most controversial issues in research ethics, not only hotly contested but also often violent. Animal rights activists have been known to break into scientific laboratories or animal breeding facilities to destroy research records, materials, equipment and buildings in protest against what they consider to be the immoral use of animals. The research community has responded to such threats by promoting the humane use of animals in research. This is inextricably linked to increasing the training of researchers to develop research projects and experimental setups that meet ethical standards and regulations for the ethical treatment of animals, as well as raising their awareness of the need to limit and minimize the number of animals used for research purposes.

Opponents of the Idea of Using Animals Give Two Main Arguments

  1. These experiments cause unnecessary and unjustified suffering to animals.
  2. Our attitude towards animals can influence how we treat people: Cruelty to animals can lead to cruelty to people.

The Scientific Community's Response to These Accusations

The defense of animal experimentation and the research community’s response to such accusations must include two equally important and complementary components:

  • Justification of the necessity of conducting experiments on animals – such experiments are important and necessary because they generate “good knowledge”. Thanks to the knowledge obtained through them, humanity has prospered and millions of human lives have been saved.
  • Continuous work to convince the public that such research is not conducted for selfish purposes and without control, but in compliance with strict ethical standards and with respect for the moral status of animals.

History of Using Animals in Research

1. Some Major Scientific Achievements Obtained Through the Use of Animals

  • Understanding the anatomy and physiology of the body (e.g., Pavlov’s experiments with dogs from the late 19th century, through which he studied the mechanisms of salivation)
  • Data on pathological changes in various diseases and the mechanisms of infection and their spread (experiments by L. Pasteur and R. Koch on the study of anthrax and tuberculosis in sheep, mice and guinea pigs)
  • Development of new technologies (e.g., cloning of mammals - Dolly the sheep, 1996)
  • Extraction of biologically active substances for the treatment or compensation of diseases (e.g., insulin for the treatment of diabetes, 1922, obtaining a vaccine against leprosy from an armadillo, etc., development of a vaccine against polio, etc.)

params.text:
2. Controversies Over the Moral Status of Animals

Although they have been going on for several centuries, intense discussions on issues related to the moral attitude towards animals and the need for protection, as well as demands for the recognition of animal rights, continue to this day. In these debates, opposing positions often clash.

Some believe that animals are not rational beings, they have no interests of their own to be respected or protected, and therefore we have no moral obligations towards them – i.e. it is completely ethically justified to use them for our own purposes and in our interest. French philosopher René Descartes (1596–1650) described animals as machines, and their behavior as the result of instincts, reflexes, and other internal mechanisms that do not involve consciousness or rationality. Therefore, we have no moral obligations towards them.

At the other side are researchers who argue that animals have at least some characteristics on the basis of which we owe them respect and moral protection and which we must consider. Jeremy Bentham (1748–1832) and John Stuart Mill (1806–1873) share the idea that animals can suffer and therefore deserve moral attitude. It is therefore wrong to use them to achieve our own ends. Developing this idea further in his book Animal Liberation (1975), Peter Singer disputes the moral permissibility of harming animals for the purpose of advancing scientific knowledge, but distinguishes between different types of animals and accordingly recognizes that some of them we do not owe protection to. This suggests that humans have a moral obligation to refrain from causing animals to suffer. Bernard Rollin (1982 in his book Animal Rights and Human Morality) argues that animals have rights that we should respect and protect. They do not have the full range of rights that humans have, but they do have rights such as the right to life and the right to health. He also points out the inadequacy of the care and husbandry provided to experimental animals, which leads to additional suffering that is not only part of the research but is also, in many cases, hostile to its aims.

params.text:
Ethical Animal Experimentation and Scientific Validity

In order the ethical side of animal experimentation to be assessed, there are a series of questions that researchers must answer before planning an animal experiment.:

panels.title: The Scientific Necessity of the Experiment

params.text: If the experiment has already been done, is it worth repeating it or not? Although it is often important to repeat new experimental findings, unnecessary repetition should be avoided.

panels.title: The Adequacy of the Animal Model

params.text:
In research protocols the species used to answer research questions are specified, as well as a rationale for choosing the specific species—how the experiment will provide evidence that is relevant to the research question.

If the research question is related to studying the mechanisms of nerve impulse conduction along axons, then the squid can be a good animal model because it has long axons that are easy to study. In addition, the knowledge gained from this model can be generalized to other species, due to their similar structure.

If we want to know whether a particular chemical agent is likely to be toxic or carcinogenic to humans, then it is important to use an animal species that is metabolically similar to the human species. For many years, researchers have more or less assumed that toxicity studies in mice can be generalized to humans, but this assumption is now being questioned. For example, researchers once thought that saccharin could cause bladder cancer in humans based on studies in which mice were fed huge doses of saccharin and then developed tumors in their bladders. However, we know that laboratory mice have a waste elimination mechanism that is different from the human mechanism. When mice eliminate saccharin, they accumulate uric acid crystals in their bladders. Humans, on the other hand, do not form these crystals. Therefore, conclusions about the carcinogenic effects of saccharin in laboratory mice probably do not apply to humans.

Should be reduced without compromising the ability to obtain useful data, while researchers must ensure that they use enough animals to obtain statistically significant data and results. Otherwise, the experiment causes unnecessary harm to the animals. This is where good statistical design and ethical practice go hand in hand.

panels.title: Efforts to Promote Animal Welfare and Reduce Harm

params.text: Taking measures to minimize pain, suffering, injury and death of animals - appropriate use of analgesia and anesthesia should be considered; humane forms of euthanasia when required by pathological findings; appropriate and sterile surgical procedures; disease control; appropriate housing conditions - nutrition, living space and exercise.

Researchers should find alternatives to animal models whenever possible, such as cell and tissue cultures and computer simulations. However, it is unlikely that researchers will be able to completely eliminate the need for animal subjects, as many complex physiological, behavioral, and developmental phenomena can only be understood in the context of a whole organism.

params.text:
The Use of Animals in Research

It is currently considered ethically justified and acceptable to use experimental animals to conduct seven main types of research:

panels.title: 1. Basic Biological, Behavioral, or Psychological Research

params.text: Formulating and testing hypotheses about fundamental theoretical questions (DNA replication mechanism, mitochondrial activity, brain functions, learning), with little attention to the practical effect of this research.

panels.title: 2. Applied Basic Biomedical and Psychological Research

params.text: Formulating and testing hypotheses about diseases, dysfunctions, genetic defects, etc., which, while not necessarily having immediate consequences for the treatment of the disease, are seen as directly related to such consequences. Also includes testing of new therapies: surgery, gene therapy, radiation therapy, burn treatment, etc. There is a spectrum, not a clear boundary between categories 1 and 2.

It differs from the above categories (especially category 2) primarily in that the research is guided not so much by well-formulated theories suggesting that a given compound may have a certain effect, but rather by exploratory, inductive testing and recording of observed effects. The main difference between this category and the others is that the goal here is the discovery of specific substances for specific purposes, rather than knowledge itself.
Aimed at increasing the productivity and efficiency of farm animals - feed trials, metabolism studies, some reproductive work and the development of agents to increase milk/meat production, etc.

Testing various consumer goods for safety, toxicity, irritation, and degree of toxicity - testing of cosmetics, food additives, herbicides, pesticides and industrial chemicals, as well as testing of drugs for toxicity, carcinogenesis, mutagenesis and teratogenesis (causing abnormalities in the development of the embryo). To some extent, this category overlaps with categories 3 and 4, but should be distinguished by the fact that (3) refers to the discovery of new drugs for humans and their testing, and (4) to cases of veterinary drugs, animal safety.
The use of animals in educational institutions and elsewhere for demonstration, dissection, surgical practice, inducing disease for demonstration purposes, high school science projects, etc.

panels.title: 7. Extraction of Drugs and Biological Products

params.text: Use of animals to extract drugs and biological products – for vaccines, blood, serum, monoclonal antibodies, etc.

params.text:
Basic Ethical Principles in Conducting Experiments with Animals

The 3Rs principle - originally proposed by Russel and Burch in 1959, and now internationally accepted by the biomedical community as a basis for the care and use of animals for research, testing, or training. The three Rs can be justified on the grounds that they minimize harm to animals and promote humane treatment in the context of animal experimentation.

Efforts to use non-animal models:

  • When it is possible to answer a research question without using an animal, then the animal should be replaced by a methodology that does not use animals, e.g. cell cultures or computer modeling.
  • Researchers should try to replace evolutionarily higher animals with animals lower in the phylogenetic tree, i.e. when it is possible to answer a scientific question using a morally “lower” animal species, it is preferable to replace the “higher” species with a lower one.

Using fewer animals for each test:

  • When it is possible to answer a research question using fewer animals, the number of animals used should be reduced (information in the literature can help determine the minimum number of animals needed to achieve meaningful data for a particular study).
  • Animal studies should not be repeated or duplicated unnecessarily.
  • Rational selection of group size, careful experimental design, maximum animal utilization, proper model selection, minimizing animal loss, and statistical analysis, if considered in the study design, can help to significantly reduce the number of animals.

Procedures should be designed and performed so that pain and suffering to the animal can be eliminated or minimized.

  • Where possible, research methods, techniques, concepts, and instruments should be refined to reduce the need for animals in research and to minimize harm to animals.
  • When possible, less invasive procedures should be used and strict attention should be paid to adequate anesthesia or analgesia. (More sophisticated monitoring equipment, such as CO2 monitors, pulse oximeters, ECG machines, and blood gas machines, are used in research settings. They allow us to ensure better physiological conditions for animals during anesthesia and surgery.).

Research protocols that use animals must address questions that have some scientific, medical, or social significance; any risks to animals must be balanced against the benefits to humans and animals.

Redundancy in animal research should be avoided whenever possible. This requires a thorough literature search to ensure that the experiment has not already been done. If it has already been done, a good enough justification for repeating the work should be provided. Avoiding redundancy is important to avoid unnecessary use of animals and waste of research resources.

According to Dr. Ronald E. Banks, this means:

  • Responsibility to animals – does not imply equality between humans and animals, but rather a commitment to practicing appropriate animal care.
  • Responsibility to the public – not only educating the public about the benefits derived from animal research, but also listening to the public’s concerns and responding to them in a calm and gentle manner with the truth.
  • Responsibility to scientific and medical integrity – optimal protocol design, sufficient database searching, peer review, and professional oversight.
  • Responsibility for appropriate stewardship of animal resources – requires careful selection of the right model system for specific scientific problems and the use of an appropriate number of animals - neither too many nor too few - to answer the question at hand.

params.text:
European Union Regulation

In European Union legislation, the use of animals for experimental purposes is regulated in DIRECTIVE 2010/63/EU OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL of 22 September 2010 on the protection of animals used for scientific purposes.

This directive establishes the following provisions:

panels.title: Animal Welfare as an EU Value

params.text: Recognises animal welfare as an EU value. Adopts the guidelines of the European Convention for the Protection of Vertebrate Animals on the care of experimental animals.

Recognises the capacity of animals to feel and express pain, suffering, distress and lasting harm. Postulates that this necessitates improving the welfare of animals used in scientific procedures by raising the minimum standards for their protection in line with the latest scientific developments.
Allows national legislation to set a higher level of protection than EU legislation.

Postulates that protection is due to all vertebrates, incl. fetal forms, invertebrates such as cyclostomatoes and cephalopods, due to their ability to feel pain, suffering, distress and permanent harm.

Enforces the principle of the three Rs. Accepts that animals have intrinsic value that must be respected. Regulates the use of primates. Introduces independent, impartial evaluation of scientific projects involving animals.

Permits the use of animals for:

  1. Basic research
  2. Translational or applied research (for the avoidance, prevention, diagnosis or treatment of diseases, impairment of health or other abnormalities or their effects on humans, animals or plants; for the assessment, detection, regulation or modification of physiological conditions in humans, animals or plants; or for the welfare of animals and the improvement of the production conditions of animals kept for agricultural purposes)
  3. Development, production or testing of the quality, efficacy and safety of medicines, food and feed products and other substances or products
  4. Protection of the natural environment in the interests of the health or well-being of humans or animals
  5. Research aimed at the conservation of species
  6. Higher education or training for the acquisition, maintenance or improvement of professional skills
  7. Forensic investigations

params.text:
Development of the Idea for the Three R's

In 2010, as an initiative of the National Centre for Replacement, Refinement and Reduction of Animals in Research (NC3Rs), the ARRIVE guidelines (Animal Research: Reporting of In Vivo Experiments) were developed and published. They are currently endorsed by a number of scientific journals and funding agencies. They ensure that animal studies are reported in sufficient detail, in addition to the scientific knowledge base.

The ARRIVE guidelines contain a checklist of 21 items (of which 10 are essential) addressing information such as the number and specific characteristics of animals used (e.g. species, sex, strain, genetic background); housing conditions; experimental, statistical and analytical methods.

The objectives are to improve the design, analysis and reporting of animal studies, maximising the information published and minimising unnecessary studies.

panels.title: The Ethical Duty to Report Failures

params.text: From an ethical perspective, it is the duty of every researcher who uses animals to seek all possible ways to reduce the number of animals used and killed. Successes are always published, but failures are rarely reported, leading to duplication of effort and the use of larger numbers of animals. This obstacle can be overcome by creating adequate databases that record both successes and failures. Knowledge of proven failures in previous experimental designs can lead to solutions that significantly reduce the number of animals used in future studies.

panels.title: Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees (IACUC)

params.text:
Their existence is regulated by both EU legislation and the regulatory framework in different countries. They have different names in different countries, such as Institutional Animal Ethics Committee, Institutional Animal Review Committee, Animal Care and Use Committee (ACUC), Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC), etc.

They have different composition, functions and responsibilities depending on local legislation, deriving their duties and powers from the law.

All protocols involving the use of animals must be reviewed and approved by the relevant committee and experiments can only begin after their written approval.

1. Review of proposed activities and projects that will use animals in teaching, testing, or research
  2. Periodically review the animal care and use program and inspect the facilities where animals are housed and used in research
  3. Investigate concerns about the use and treatment of animals in teaching, testing, and research at the institution

params.text:
Case Study: Testing a New Drug on Dogs

(from Responsible Conduct of Research, Adil E. Shamoo and David B. Resnik, Print publication date: 2009, Print ISBN-13: 9780195368246, page 233, DOI:10.1093/acprof:oso/9780195368246.003.0011, Published to Oxford Scholarship Online: May 2009)

A researcher plans to test a new analgesic drug on dogs. The drug may be useful in relieving pain associated with severe burns. To conduct the experiment, the researcher will use two groups of 12 dogs each - an experimental group and a control group. Both groups will receive a burn on their back. Both will receive treatment for the burn, but only one group will receive the study drug.

The plan is also to try to measure the level of pain and discomfort by touching the burn to elicit a response, such as behavioral signals, heart rate, and blood pressure changes.

If you are a member of an institutional animal use committee, would you approve this experiment? Why or why not?

Actions: In this case, the ethical concerns can be described as follows: is it ethically justified to conduct this study, given that it involves inflicting a bodily wound and subsequently causing further harm?

Motivations: From a scientific point of view, the motivation for conducting this study is clear. It is related to the search for new knowledge regarding the effectiveness of a new drug with application in veterinary medicine. The aim is to establish whether this new drug is more effective than the already applied ones.

Dilemmas: The ethical dilemma is whether it is justified to cause suffering to animals (possible harm and discomfort) in the name of creating a possible good that will benefit many other suffering animals in the future.

Ethical Issues

Primary Issues: basic criteria for admissibility of scientific research

Secondary Issues: conditions for ethical conduct of animal research

Applicable Ethical Principles: ethical principles when working with laboratory animals - 3R

Discussion Questions

  • Does this study meet the criteria for scientific research?
  • Does this study meet the criteria for ethical animal research?
  • What type of animal research does it refer to?
  • Were the 3R principles followed in the study design?

Reflection Section

If you were a member of the committee, would you approve this study? What design changes would you recommend and why?

Suggested Resolution and Best Practices

One of the main activities of the committees for the care and use of animals for scientific purposes is the review and evaluation of the proposed experimental protocols. For this purpose, the members of the committees must know the ethical standards applicable to such activities, but also be aware of the regulatory framework at European, national and institutional levels.

The study proposed for evaluation falls into the group of studies related to the development of drugs and therapeutic agents intended for veterinary medicine. In principle, conducting this study is justified and necessary, since it is new and the test substance has not been tested to date. Such type of studies are permitted by European legislation. In addition, if positive results from the study are produced, namely higher effectiveness than other drugs, it is expected that the drug will be put into use, which will bring direct benefits to all animals on which it will be administered. In this case, testing on animals is fully justified and necessary, since it concerns a product with future veterinary use and its effect cannot be adequately assessed in any other way, without the use of animals. I.e. in this particular case, no alternative can be proposed to replace the experimental model (dogs).

In this case, the use of dogs is proposed, to which many authors attribute a high moral status. It stems from their relationship with humanity (they have accompanied us since ancient times, we have a sentimental attitude towards them and use them not only as guards, helpers, etc., but also as companions). Due to this high status, it is morally acceptable to use them in a limited set of experiments and to avoid their use in others, in which it is ethically justified/acceptable to use animals with a lower moral status (such as frogs, fruit flies/Drosophila or worms/Caenorhabditis elegans), which are lower in the evolutionary tree. The motivation for choosing the specific object in this case is the future use on animals of the same species, which fully justifies the choice of the experimental model.

The adequacy of the proposed number of animals used can only be assessed by comparison with other similar studies. The author of the study should provide such information in the documentation submitted to the evaluation committee. If there is data in the literature that similar studies have been conducted with a much larger number of animals of the same species (dogs) in the experimental and control groups, then the number proposed in this case would not provide sufficient statistical reliability of the results. This is immoral, because pain and suffering would be caused in vain, and resources would be spent, without leading to the generation of usable and reliable scientific results. Conversely, if a smaller number of animals were used in similar studies (which is unlikely in this case), then increasing the sample size would also be ethically unjustified.

A serious problem in the study proposed for evaluation is the experimental design, which includes intentional damage (burning) in research conditions. A replacement could be proposed with an experiment conducted in veterinary clinics, where the new drug would be tested on animals admitted there for burn treatment. A possible justification for the originally proposed version of the trial would be the relatively small number of animals injured in such a way and the associated need for a long period of time to collect the necessary amount of data. Such justifications are not ethically sound. If evidence from veterinary practice shows that very few animals suffer such injuries and there is already a treatment available to relieve this pain, a sufficiently good argument needs to be presented to justify the proposed experimental design. This could be the existence of preliminary data that the new treatment is much better and more effective than the existing ones. This would also justify shortening the time frame for the study, in order to have it approved and put into use as soon as possible.

Another aspect of the study that also raises questions is the planned additional infliction of pain. The text of the case study does not make it clear exactly how it will be induced. It is described that it will be through touch, which is too general. It could be touching with a hand or some kind of instrument. Obtaining relevant data on the degree of pain requires that it be caused in the same way, with the same force on each of the animals. Otherwise, the data obtained, regardless of the described ways in which an attempt will be made to quantify them, will be relative and not comparable. But since this is a test of a pain relieving drug, it is clear that such manipulation cannot be avoided. Without collecting this information, the entire study loses its meaning, which makes it unacceptable from an ethical point of view. The proposed text does not describe exactly what the pain stimulus will be and how it will be applied. In order this part of the experiment to be approved, additional information must be provided to assess whether it will lead to the production of valid, applicable data.

An ethical requirement in the design of animal experiments is that discomfort should be limited to the amount which is unavoidable for the conduct of a scientifically valuable study, and that unrelieved or induced pain should last only as long as is necessary to achieve the scientific objectives. If the pain caused cannot be relieved and the animals are experiencing significant suffering as a result of the experimental procedure, they should be humanely killed at the end of the procedure or, if appropriate, during the procedure.

The criteria used to terminate experimental studies early in order to avoid or eliminate unrelieved pain and/or distress are called humane endpoints. They should ensure that the objectives of the study will be achieved, even though the study is terminated early. Ideally, humane endpoints are sought that can be used to terminate studies before the onset of pain and distress. Endpoints are established for both scientific and humane reasons.

In this case, animals in both the control and experimental groups will be given pain-relieving treatment that does not involve causing uncompensated suffering. Therefore, the formulation of the conditions for early termination of the experiment should be related not to a description of the conditions under which the animals will be humanely killed. Conditions should be formulated under which it is ethically and scientifically justified to terminate the experiment on the basis of the data already obtained, without using the complete number of animals intended. Such termination would be justified in two cases:

  • if the test drug does not produce the desired effect (does not relieve the pain caused), or
  • if the test drug has a much stronger positive effect than the drug it is being compared to.

In both cases, early termination of the trial would limit the suffering of animals receiving the less effective treatment. However, the experimental protocol should clearly state the minimum/maximum number of animals required to show or not show an effect before the experiment can be stopped.

The qualifications of the team conducting the study are also important. The care of the animals, as well as the conduct and reporting of the experimental procedures, should be carried out by people who are not only appropriately qualified (trained caretakers, veterinary staff and scientists), but they should also be aware of the specific physiological characteristics of the individual species they are working with. The latter is extremely important in order to be able to recognize the symptoms and manifestations of pain and distress, which differ between species, and to respond appropriately, in accordance with the procedures outlined in the experimental protocols or good research practices.

params.text:
Summary and Key Takeaways

Congratulations on completing this module on The Use of Animals in Research! Here are the key takeaways from your learning journey:

  • Historical context: Animal research has contributed to major scientific breakthroughs, from Pavlov’s experiments to the development of life-saving vaccines and insulin therapy.
  • Moral status debate: The ethical debate spans centuries – from Descartes’ view of animals as machines to Singer’s and Rollin’s arguments for animal rights and moral consideration based on sentience and suffering.
  • Scientific validity: Ethical experimentation requires demonstrating scientific necessity, selecting appropriate animal models, using proper sample sizes, minimizing harm, and exploring alternatives.
  • Seven categories of use: Animal research spans basic research, applied biomedical research, drug development, food and fiber research, safety testing, education, and biological product extraction.
  • The 3Rs: Replacement, Reduction, and Refinement are the internationally accepted foundation for ethical animal use, supplemented by additional Rs: Relevance, Redundancy avoidance, and Responsibility.
  • EU regulation: Directive 2010/63/EU establishes comprehensive protections for animals used in research, recognizing their intrinsic value and capacity to feel pain.
  • ARRIVE guidelines: Developed by NC3Rs, these ensure transparent and detailed reporting of animal studies to maximize information and minimize unnecessary duplication.
  • IACUC oversight: Institutional committees review, inspect, and investigate all protocols involving animals to ensure ethical and regulatory compliance.
  • Humane endpoints: Criteria for early termination of studies should be established to avoid or minimize unrelieved pain and distress.

As researchers, educators, and committee members, you play a vital role in ensuring that animal research is conducted responsibly, ethically, and with the highest scientific standards. Every decision you make regarding animal use has both scientific and moral dimensions. Continue to apply the principles you have learned here to contribute to a more responsible and humane research community.
